challenges.title: Working Time Regulations, rest periods and data protection

items.title: Keeping the 48-hour week & opt-out under control
items.text: The Working Time Regulations 1998 cap average weekly working time at 48 hours, calculated over a standard 17-week reference period — extendable by agreement. Staff can opt out in writing, which makes manual tracking even harder.

items.title: Guaranteeing daily & weekly rest periods
items.text: The WTR require at least 11 consecutive hours of rest per 24 hours and 24 uninterrupted hours per 7-day period (Reg. 10 & 11) — error-prone to track by hand across rotating shifts.

items.title: Biometric time tracking as a data protection risk
items.text: In February 2024, the ICO took enforcement action against Serco Leisure after facial recognition and fingerprint clocking systems at 38 sites processed data on over 2,000 employees without a lawful basis — a warning sign for any time-tracking solution.

rulesCalendar.title: A calendar for every nation
rulesCalendar.text: Bank holidays are anything but uniform across the United Kingdom: England & Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland each observe their own set of statutory holidays, and individual councils add local holidays on top — such as Glasgow Fair Monday, the third Monday in July. Klacks handles exactly what simple tools get wrong.

items.title: Three nations, three sets of holidays
items.text: 2 January and St Andrew's Day (30 November) are bank holidays only in Scotland; St Patrick's Day (17 March) and the Battle of the Boyne — known as "the Twelfth" (12 July) — only in Northern Ireland: pre-configured and ready to use.

items.title: Mix calendars
items.text: A care, security or logistics business with sites in London, Edinburgh and Belfast runs all three calendars side by side — including bank holiday premiums and the reduced staff availability on days when nurseries and schools close in only one nation.

items.title: Binding or purely informational
items.text: For each calendar, you decide whether a bank holiday affects hours & premiums — or simply appears as a reminder.

rulesCalendar.imageCaption: Real rules from Klacks: every holiday rule carries a country and a region, and the list can be filtered by both — freely extensible.

solutions.title: How Klacks takes the load off UK businesses
solutions.subtitle: From automatic rest-period control to time tracking without biometrics — everything works together.

items.title: 48-hour limit & opt-out kept in view
items.text: Klacks monitors the rolling 17-week average of working time live, correctly factoring in each employee's start date, and warns before the 48-hour limit under WTR Reg. 4 is exceeded — while flagging who is working beyond it under an opt-out. On request, Klacks hard-blocks a breach in automatic planning; with manual planning it stays at a warning. Fully traceable for any inspection.

items.title: Rest periods checked automatically
items.text: The 11-hour daily rest and 24-hour weekly rest under WTR Reg. 10 & 11 are factored into every automatic shift plan — and any breach is immediately made visible.

items.title: Time tracking without the biometric risk
items.text: Klacks records working time without needing facial recognition or fingerprints — which removes the very trigger that led the ICO to step in at Serco Leisure.

items.title: Installed on your premises: data on your servers
items.text: Klacks runs on your own infrastructure, and you choose the AI model yourself — optionally locally hosted, so that no staff data goes to external AI providers. This supports the requirements of UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018.

items.title: Keeping an eye on the Employment Rights Act 2025
items.text: The Employment Rights Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025 and will in future govern advance notice periods for shifts and compensation for cancelled shifts — the exact thresholds have yet to be set. You can already store a minimum notice period as a planning deadline today; Klacks uses it to calculate when the schedule must be ready. Klacks does not calculate compensation for cancelled shifts.

items.title: Klacksy: rule-based, not a black box
items.text: The built-in AI assistant Klacksy understands instructions in everyday language and controls Klacks; the rule-based planning engine calculates the plan — traceable through defined rules, not an opaque AI decision.

items.title: Test plan changes risk-free
items.text: Before a plan change goes live, you can run it through as an isolated copy — the 11-hour daily rest under WTR Reg. 10 and premiums are calculated live exactly as in the real plan. Only once everything checks out do you apply the variant; until then, your live schedule stays untouched. This lets you prepare a suitable scenario in advance for foreseeable situations — such as a staff member calling in sick or a sudden spike in orders — so you're ready to act immediately when it matters, instead of improvising under time pressure. There's no artificial limit on the number of scenarios — create as many as your planning needs.

klacksy.title: Klacksy: the assistant built into your team
klacksy.text: Klacksy isn't a bolted-on marketing chatbot — it's embedded directly in the Klacks interface. Staff and schedulers use chat to check shift times or clarify availability. A built-in skills and rules system ensures Klacksy always makes traceable suggestions — never a black-box decision. For businesses with strict data protection requirements, the AI model can also be hosted locally.

example.title: The 48-hour week and rest periods, at a glance
example.text: Klacks automatically detects when an employee is approaching the 48-hour limit in the rolling 17-week average or a rest period under WTR Reg. 10 would fall short, and suggests the adjustment straight away — no manual recalculating required.
